claims.text: Near-equiatomic multi-element nanoparticles have maximum configurational entropy.
Maximum configurational entropy slows atomic diffusion in these nanoparticles.
Slower atomic diffusion prevents phase segregation during high-temperature catalytic and thermoelectric operation.
The initial near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles have a homogeneous elemental distribution.
An equiatomic solid solution forms a stabilized lattice with sluggish diffusion dynamics.
A near-equiatomic configuration creates a stable, highly disordered lattice.
The highly disordered lattice resists atomic migration and phase segregation.
Even slight deviations from equiatomic composition reduce entropy stabilization.
Reduced entropy stabilization caused by compositional deviation enhances atomic diffusion.
Compositional deviation increases the risk of dealloying or phase separation during high-temperature operation.
Near-equiatomic nanoparticles will undergo less grain growth and phase segregation than deliberately composition-perturbed nanoparticles under identical high-temperature conditions.
Near-equiatomic nanoparticles will retain greater chemical uniformity than composition-perturbed nanoparticles under identical high-temperature conditions.
The proposed entropy-mediated mechanism applies broadly to multi-element solid-solution nanoparticles across the stated catalytic and thermoelectric temperature ranges.
Melting, severe dealloying, large departures from equiatomic composition, or extremely oxidizing environments can activate alternative stabilization or degradation pathways.
